newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. may have retaliated against Time Warner: Judge.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. may have retaliated against Time Warner: Judge.

text.p: A federal judge said Wednesday there was evidence showing that New York City had retaliated against Time Warner Inc. by planning to air Rupert Murdoch's Fox News on a city-run cable channel.
However, U.S. District Judge Denise Cote did not rule on Time Warner's request for an order blocking the plan and took arguments under advisement.
Cote made her comments during closing arguments in a hearing that began Monday to determine whether her earlier temporary order against the city will be extended.

The dispute centers on the role of the city's five stations, known as Crosswalks. New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani decided to place the new 24-hour Fox programming on one of the Crosswalks channels after Time Warner rejected it. He also plans to run Bloomberg Television News, which also is not aired by Time Warner.

Time Warner, which serves 1.1 million customers in New York, sued the city alleging that New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani was acting on behalf of Murdoch's News Corp. Ltd., which owns the New York Post and WNYW-TV. It said in its suit that the city was acting as Murdoch's "latest political puppet."
"The retaliatory facts are very much in play," Cote told lawyers representing New York City.

But Paul Crotty, corporation counsel, disagreed. Giuliani has said that he had sided with Fox because it is the only 24-hour news channel based in New York City and contributes more than 1,000 jobs to the economy.
"Our motivation started out with economic development. ..I don't see how there could be retaliation.," Crotty said.

In its suit, Time Warner alleged that the city's plan violates its free speech rights because the city is interfering with its editorial discretion by trying to force it to carry the two news channels.
"This is a classic First Amendment five alarm fire," said Stuart Gold, a lawyer representing Time Warner.
"The government is acting under the cover of darkness to insert its choice of news programming into the homes of millions of New York viewers," he said.
Time Warner also alleged that the plan violated its franchise agreement with the city. It argued that the agreement provides that the city-run channels only be used for non-commercial purposes.
Time Warner also alleged that the Federal Cable Act prohibits governmental stations from being used for commercial use.
